article_title: Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development
citation: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101
title: Knowledge Debt: a developer-level analogue of Technical Debt incurred when agents change code the developer does not fully understand
description: Knowledge Debt is the article's central explanatory construct: "a developer-level analogue to Technical Debt, incurred when an agent makes changes to the codebase that the developer does not fully understand". Like Technical Debt, it "compounds silently and surfaces only when independent capability is required, at which point repayment through relearning becomes costly". The authors propose operationalizing it as a measurable construct as future work.
requirements: Applies in settings where developers delegate code changes to AI agents whose reasoning the developer does not fully verify.
constraints: The article presents Knowledge Debt as a posited construct; empirical operationalization is explicitly future work.
target_learners: Professional software developers using AI coding agents
target_learning_goals: Maintaining independent debugging, adaptation, and extension capability while working with AI-generated code
examples: The paper frames the accumulating gap between AI-generated code and developer understanding, building on prior work in cognitive offloading and skill atrophy.
key_sources: Rohit Mehra, Samdyuti Suri, Prithviraj K Tagadinamani, Kapil Singi, Vikrant Kaulgud, Adam P. Burden. (2026). Agents That Teach: Towards Designing Incidental Learning Back into AI-Assisted Software Development. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.06101

article_title: Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education
citation: Esse Ciego, Shubbhi Taneja, Wilson Wong, and Amanpreet Kapoor. (2026). Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28203
title: Knowlify AI video generation platform
description: Knowlify is a conversational AI video generation system that "enables users to create explainer-style videos from natural language prompts and uploaded source documents." Users provide a prompt, optionally upload materials, and select options such as video length and narrator voice; the system generates a narration script, scene-level storyboard, and voiceovers that can be reviewed and edited before final production. In this study, three 3-minute Markdown videos were generated from GitHub's official documentation, costing about $50-60 and at most 25 minutes per video.
requirements: A natural language prompt and optionally uploaded source documents; configurable options such as video length and narrator voice; human time for review, verification, and editing before final production.
target_learning_goals: instructional explainer videos for programming concepts such as Markdown
examples: The study authors uploaded GitHub's official Markdown formatting documentation as a PDF and generated three 3-minute videos, with generation taking 3 minutes 48 seconds on average per video.
key_sources: Esse Ciego, Shubbhi Taneja, Wilson Wong, and Amanpreet Kapoor. (2026). Student Perceptions and Preferences Regarding AI-Generated Instructional Videos in Computing Education. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28203

citation: Marzano, D. (2025). Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) in Teaching and Learning Processes at the K-12 Level: A Systematic Review. Technology, Knowledge and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10758-025-09853-7
title: Lee's Know-Build-Critique (KBC) model for guiding students' conscious use of GAI
description: The review reports that Lee (2023) proposes the Know-Build-Critique (KBC) model "to guide students in the conscious use of GAI". The model emphasizes "understanding the capabilities and limitations of technology, integrating new information critically and responsibly, and ethically evaluating generated information". It responds to the review's argument that adoption of GAI requires training students who not only use, but also actively build and critique knowledge, capable of identifying ethical issues and reflecting on AI's social implications.

constraints: Attributed in the review to Lee (2023); the review does not report empirical evaluation of the model
target_learners: K-12 students using generative AI tools
target_learning_goals: AI literacy, critical and ethical evaluation of AI-generated information
examples: The review cites the model as a proposed guide for conscious GAI use in its literature overview

article_title: How Human-Centered Is AI-Aided Learning in Education?
citation: Katia Tödt, Corinne Büching, and Bastian Granas. (2026). Digital Education and Innovation: Objectives and Conceptual Classification of the Volume. In Digital Education and Innovation. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-26816-7_1
title: Knowledge triangle of research, education and innovation adapted to the educational context
description: The chapter adapts the innovation-economics 'knowledge triangle' to education as the volume's organising framework. It argues that education in this model 'encompasses the entire multi-level system of education', including administration and practice, not only university teaching. The triangle visualises interactions between research, education and innovation and frames transformation processes as interdisciplinary and innovation-oriented.
requirements: A broader understanding of education that incorporates the control, organisational, and action levels of the education system
constraints: The classic interpretation ties innovation to economic exploitation of research results, which the authors explicitly widen for the educational context
target_learning_goals: understanding and designing digital education innovation processes
examples: The chapter uses the adapted triangle to contextualise the volume's four thematic sections and to analyse why transfer of research knowledge into practice has been insufficient

article_title: PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning
citation: Yu Liu, Zeming Liu, Tianle Zhang, Zihao Cheng, Yuhang Guo, Kehai Chen, Min Zhang, Yunhong Wang, Haifeng Wang. (2026). PersonaPath: Towards Knowledge-Centric Personalized Learning Path Planning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.18861
title: Knowledge-Centric (KC) paradigm for learning path planning
description: The KC paradigm contrasts with the dominant Exercise-Centric (EC) recommendation paradigm: instead of inferring the next exercise from item-level interaction logs, "a Knowledge-Centric (KC) paradigm, which decides what knowledge a learner should study and in what order." A KC planner reads each learner's progress and goal, selects knowledge from a structured knowledge space, and orders it into a path respecting prerequisite relations among concepts. Evaluation requires explicit learner personas, long-term goals, and curriculum-scale prerequisite structures together, since the goal sets the destination, the mastery state the starting point, and the prerequisite graph the routes between them.
requirements: Evaluation requires explicit learner personas, long-term goals, and curriculum-scale prerequisite structures jointly
constraints: Existing benchmarks primarily support exercise recommendation and rarely jointly provide these components, per the article
target_learners: learners with similar exercise records but different goals
target_learning_goals: selecting and ordering knowledge, not exercises, toward an explicit target
examples: Figure 1 contrasts two students with identical correctness records who need different paths because their targets differ

article_title: Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI
citation: Luis Marquez-Carpintero, Alberto Lopez-Sellers, Miguel Cazorla. (2025). Simulating Students with Large Language Models: A Review of Architecture, Mechanisms, and Role Modelling in Education with Generative AI. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.06078
title: Three-strategy taxonomy for modelling student knowledge in Simulated Students: direct prompts, knowledge tracing, and knowledge graphs with heuristics
description: The review organises knowledge modelling for LLM-based Simulated Students into three strategies. In direct prompt-based simulation, "Knowledge levels, common mistakes, or learning styles are directly defined within the LLM prompt", which is easy and customisable but risks overly idealised behaviour. Knowledge tracing tracks mastery of knowledge components over time with models such as DKT, DKVMN, AKT, or LLM-KT, offering strong prediction and real-time adaptation at the cost of technical complexity and data needs. Knowledge graphs and heuristics define the knowledge state with structured representations and explicit rules, giving high interpretability but requiring extensive manual curation. The review uses this taxonomy to structure its analysis of how simulated agents acquire, forget, and apply knowledge.
requirements: Direct prompt simulation relies heavily on prompt quality; knowledge tracing requires large datasets; knowledge graphs require extensive manual curation
constraints: Knowledge tracing interpretation can be challenging; knowledge graphs struggle with dynamic learning processes
target_learners: virtual simulated students in educational research
target_learning_goals: representing learner knowledge states, mastery, and misconceptions in simulation
examples: The review summarises the three strategies with advantages and limitations in Table 1, and describes Generative Students sampling mastered, confused and unknown knowledge components to craft learner personas

article_title: Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education
citation: Stephan Vonschallen, Karim Kaufmann, Dominique Oberle, Friederike Eyssel, Theresa Schmiedel. (2026). Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22345
title: Knowledge-Based Design (KBD): responsible tutoring behavior in generative social robots depends on the robot's self-, user-, and context-knowledge
description: KBD is a design framework holding that responsible robot tutoring behavior depends on what knowledge the robot possesses, organized into three types. The article states the underlying assumption that "responsible robot behavior depends on the availability ofself-,user-, andcontext-knowledge". Self-knowledge covers the robot's role (default study buddy), friendliness, conscientiousness, and assertiveness; user-knowledge covers learner-specific information such as goals, motivation type, emotional state, and background, with privacy and informed consent; context-knowledge covers official learning materials, course information, educational strategies, and optionally the physical environment. The framework was derived from a qualitative interview study with university students and lecturers and operationalized in Teachy Mini.
requirements: The robot must possess the specified self-, user-, and context-knowledge for responsible behavior to manifest; the framework specifies informational prerequisites rather than abstract ethical principles.
constraints: The 'course information' requirement applies to interactions over longer periods and was not integrated in the single-session prototype; 'physical learning environment' received only mixed support due to privacy concerns.
target_learners: university students in higher education learning lecture content
target_learning_goals: responsible and effective tutoring of lecture content, including factual accuracy, transparency, personalization, and pedagogically appropriate support
examples: Teachy Mini operationalized selected KBD requirements via dynamic system prompting, retrieval-augmented generation over uploaded lecture slides, and stateful prompt orchestration with regex-detected dialogue states.
key_sources: Stephan Vonschallen, Karim Kaufmann, Dominique Oberle, Friederike Eyssel, Theresa Schmiedel. (2026). Teachy Mini: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of a Knowledge-Based Generative Social Robot for Higher Education. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22345

article_title: VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding
citation: Ruqi Sun, Jiaping Li, Wenhui Tao, Ximing Zheng, Yuefeng Tan, Jiahao Wei, and Yuxin Ma. (2026). VeriForge: Mitigating Latent Knowledge Gaps in Narrative Drafting via Mixed-Initiative Scaffolding. https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.09698
title: Present retrieved domain knowledge as structured, source-traceable raw material rather than finished prose to preserve authorial ownership
description: The article recommends that AI writing support deliver discovered domain facts as structured raw material linked to its exact source passage, rather than near-final generated prose. Participants distrusted AI-generated prose partly because it threatened their voice — one described generic AI vocabulary as carrying a "plastic texture" — while facts traced to a specific primary source felt trustworthy enough to adopt directly. Presenting knowledge as raw ingredients for active synthesis is positioned as the lever that restores trust while preserving authorial agency over narrative voice.
requirements: Retrieved knowledge must be linked to its exact source passage, preserving verifiability
constraints: The authors note this interpretation draws on participants' retrospective comparisons with prior tools rather than a controlled manipulation within their study
target_learners: Fiction writers using AI assistance for domain-specific drafting
target_learning_goals: Integrating domain knowledge into prose while retaining authorial voice and ownership
examples: VeriForge's Knowledge Cards separate an AI-generated description from a quoted source passage, and participants like P05 used the system exclusively for technique names and historical facts but refused to let it touch his combat scenes

article_title: Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader
citation: deWinstanley, P. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2004). Processing strategies and the generation effect: Implications for making a better reader. Memory & Cognition, 32(6), 945-955. https://doi.org/10.3758/BF03194854
title: Metacognitive knowledge-updating account: learners change encoding strategies only after experiencing differential performance consequences
description: The article interprets its results via Dunlosky and Hertzog's knowledge-updating framework and the metacognitive literature on illusions of competence, in which "learners are not very accurate in taking such readings and often suffer from what has been called illusions of comprehension or competence." Individuals are assumed not to update beliefs about encoding-strategy effectiveness "unless they become aware of the consequential performance differences for information processed with different strategies." Only participants who experienced both generating and reading on the same test upgraded their processing of read items.
requirements: Learners must directly experience the performance consequences of different encoding strategies within the same test context
constraints: Learners are typically unable to judge a strategy's efficacy during its execution and do not switch strategies without experiencing relative effectiveness
target_learning_goals: adopting more effective encoding strategies for reading
examples: Experiment 2 participants who generated first but never saw both item types on one test failed to appreciate the mnemonic benefit of generating and did not change their processing of read items

article_title: Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry
citation: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a
title: Knowledge-transforming model of writing as a mode of learning in science
description: The article contrasts traditional writing, compatible with the knowledge-telling model and emphasizing knowledge transmission and rote memorization, with non-traditional writing aligned with the knowledge-transforming model (Bereiter & Scardamalia, 1987). In knowledge-transforming writing, students consider prior knowledge, think about the meaning of new concepts, and plan how to communicate meaning to an audience. This occurs in an interactive-constructivist environment emphasizing individual and social knowledge construction, and provides a context for translating between everyday, audience, and science languages.
requirements: An interactive-constructivist learning environment emphasizing both individual and social construction of knowledge, plus influence of prior understandings on new learning
constraints: Traditional writing contexts where students copy teacher or textbook content do not engage the knowledge-transforming processes; the article notes much classroom writing does not go beyond copying
target_learning_goals: conceptual understanding of science concepts
translation between everyday and scientific language
negotiation of ideas
examples: Students writing to younger students and peers moved between everyday language and technical language, unpacking science understandings, while students writing to the teacher tended to use more science information to show what they know
key_sources: Kingir, S. (2013). Using Non-traditional Writing as a Tool in Learning Chemistry. Eurasia Journal of Mathematics, Science & Technology Education, 9(2), 101-114. https://doi.org/10.12973/eurasia.2013.922a

article_title: Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?
citation: Henk G. Schmidt & Jerome I. Rotgans. (2021). Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09539-9
title: Knowledge-deprivation account: situational interest and epistemic curiosity share one knowledge-gap mechanism
description: The knowledge-deprivation account holds that both situational interest and epistemic curiosity arise when a person confronts a problem they cannot immediately explain, experiences a gap between what they know and need to know, and is motivated to close it; acquiring relevant knowledge satisfies the drive and the motivation subsides. The article summarizes Rotgans and Schmidt's version: "(a) Confronted with a problem not immediately understood, a person engages in an attempt to retrieve knowledge from long-term memory" and "(c) This awareness of a knowledge deficit leads to increased situational interest for information that may help eliminating the deficit". The article argues the same mechanism explains epistemic curiosity, treating the two constructs as "identical twins".
requirements: A problem or triggering event the learner cannot immediately understand
The learner must become aware of a knowledge deficit
Relevant explanatory knowledge must be available to close the gap
constraints: The article notes findings are preliminary and need further confirmation
Situational interest may also be aroused by contexts other than knowledge-gap confrontation, which would broaden the concept beyond the account's boundaries
target_learning_goals: motivating engagement with new subject matter
driving knowledge acquisition in response to problems
examples: Study 2 aroused both measures with the Mpemba effect problem in treatment students and satiated them with an evaporation text
key_sources: Henk G. Schmidt & Jerome I. Rotgans. (2021). Epistemic Curiosity and Situational Interest: Distant Cousins or Identical Twins?. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-020-09539-9

article_title: An Excel sheet for inferring children’s number-knower levels from give-N data
citation: Negen, J., Sarnecka, B. W., & Lee, M. D. (2011). An Excel sheet for inferring children's number-knower levels from give-N data. Behavior Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-011-0134-4
title: Knower-LevelEstimater.xls — an Excel tool for Bayesian-style knower-level inference
description: A Microsoft Excel sheet, available at www.cogsci.uci.edu/cogdev/Negen/Knower-LevelEstimater.xls, that computes an approximation of the full Bayesian model's knower-level inference. The user enters question and response pairs (each in the range 1 to 15) and optional prior weights for knower levels; the sheet automatically calculates the likelihood of each pair conditional on each knower level and outputs posterior probabilities for the six knower levels, plus log-likelihoods and a graph.
requirements: Data entries must be in the range of 1 to 15; the sheet handles one child's data at a time; the child must have had exactly 15 items available to give
constraints: The article states the sheet is only appropriate for experiments in which the child had exactly 15 items to give, and if the child was asked for more than 15 items some other method of analysis must be used
target_learners: young children completing the give-N task
target_learning_goals: estimating a child's number-knower level from give-N task data
examples: In the worked example, a child asked for one through five and giving 1, 2, 3, 3, and 6 with equal priors yields about 60% posterior confidence that the child is a 2-knower

article_title: Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education
citation: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656
title: Knowledge integration instructional pattern: Elicit ideas, Add new ideas, Distinguish among ideas, Reflect on and integrate ideas
description: This is the instructional pattern structuring activities in the knowledge integration design framework for science curriculum projects (Slotta & Linn, 2009) as implemented in the WISE global climate change project. "Each activity starts with eliciting the ideas that students already hold. Subsequently, students get the opportunity to add new ideas and distinguish among ideas by searching and critiquing Web-based evidence, exploring provided simulations or interactive graphs, and discussing with peers. Finally, students are asked to reﬂect on these ideas in order to integrate them into their repertoire of ideas." The pattern is crossed with four knowledge integration principles: making science accessible, making thinking visible, helping students learn from others, and promoting autonomy.
requirements: Web-based evidence sources, simulations, or interactive graphs for students to search, critique, and explore
Peer discussion opportunities such as classroom debates
target_learners: Secondary school science students across achievement levels and academic tracks
target_learning_goals: Integrated, coherent understanding of scientific topics
Inquiry skills
Interest in science
examples: Table 1 maps the four principles and four pattern phases to project activities such as calculating students' ecological footprint, analyzing CO2 emissions trends in Gapminder World, and an online classroom debate between believers and nonbelievers
key_sources: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656

article_title: Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education
citation: Annelies Raes, Tammy Schellens, and Bram De Wever. (2013). Web-based Collaborative Inquiry to Bridge Gaps in Secondary Science Education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2013.836656
title: Knowledge integration approach to science learning
description: Knowledge integration is an approach to science learning conceptualized by the Technology Enhanced Learning in Science community, contrasted with the absorption approach of recalling isolated bits of information. It "can be deﬁned as the process of incorporating new information into a body of existing knowledge by guiding students to engage in inquiry (Linn & Eylon, 2011)." It builds on evidence that every student brings a repertoire of rich, confusing, and intriguing ideas to the science class and needs to link their ideas to new ideas and use evidence to sort through alternative ideas. In this study it served as the design basis for the WISE curriculum project and for outcome measures evaluating whether students could link and connect ideas using evidence.
requirements: Instruction that elicits students' existing ideas and provides evidence for sorting among alternative ideas
target_learning_goals: Knowledge acquisition as integrated understanding rather than recall of isolated facts
Inquiry skills including diagnosing problems, critiquing experiments, and forming coherent arguments
examples: The WISE global climate change project activities were designed according to the knowledge integration instructional pattern and its four principles

article_title: Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools
citation: Frank Fischer, Heinz Mandl. (2005). Knowledge Convergence in Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning: The Role of External Representation Tools. The Journal of the Learning Sciences, 14(3), pp.405-441. https://telearn.hal.science/hal-00190855
title: Knowledge convergence as a two-dimensional construct: convergence of collaborative process (resource use) versus convergence of individual outcomes
description: The article frames knowledge convergence in computer-supported collaborative learning along two distinguishable dimensions: convergence in what learners do during collaboration (their use of knowledge resources) and convergence in what they know afterwards (individual outcomes, further split into factual and application-oriented knowledge). The study's design, varying "the type of external representation (content-specific vs. content-independent) and the collaboration condition (videoconferencing vs. face-to-face)", is built to measure these dimensions separately, and its central finding is that they diverge: strong process convergence coexists with low outcome convergence.
requirements: Measuring convergence requires assessing both resource use during collaboration and individual knowledge outcomes after collaboration, as the study does.
constraints: Outcome convergence was found to be rather low in this study, and the process-outcome relation was examined only exploratorily.
target_learning_goals: factual knowledge
application-oriented knowledge
examples: The study operationalized convergence by comparing learning partners' use of knowledge resources during collaboration and their individual knowledge outcomes after collaboration under four conditions.

article_title: A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education
citation: Chen, B. (2024). A framework for infrastructuring sustainable innovations in education. Journal of the Learning Sciences. https://doi.org/10.1080/10508406.2024.2320159
title: Knowledge Building pedagogy and Knowledge Forum as a running case of infrastructuring challenges
description: Knowledge Building (KB) is a long-standing learning theory and pedagogy that supports learning by fostering continual idea improvement in a community, supported by digital technologies such as Knowledge Forum. The article uses KB initiatives worldwide as illustrative cases across all six IMPROV areas, noting that "heavy reliance on researchers creates challenges for sustainability" and that friction with existing education systems arises as KB enters new contexts.
requirements: Sustaining KB involves building infrastructures at multiple levels, including classrooms, schools, and regional and international networks
constraints: Emphasis on ongoing researcher involvement in teacher-researcher teams creates sustainability challenges; tensions arise with prescribed curriculum mandates and assessment systems
target_learning_goals: fostering continual idea improvement in knowledge-creating communities
examples: KB sites in Canada, Brazil, China, Italy, and Singapore have reported coherence-making activities; the Curriculum-Ideas Analytics tool maps student discussions onto curricular objectives

article_title: Classical dialogs in CSCL
citation: Gerry Stahl & Friedrich Hesse. (2009). Classical dialogs in CSCL. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 4. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-009-9071-y
title: Distinction of knowledge creation (community improvement of ideas) from knowledge sharing (transmission) and knowledge construction (individual constructionist)
description: van Aalst clarifies often-confused terminology of alternative theories of learning. title: Knowledge Catalyser discussion forum scaffolding metacognition through voting, annotating, critiquing, and revising postings

article_title: Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts
citation: Gerry Stahl, Ulrike Cress, Nancy Law & Sten Ludvigsen. (2014). Analyzing the multidimensional construction of knowledge in diverse contexts. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. (2014) 9:1–6. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-014-9189-4
title: Framing online discussion as a multi-user knowledge-building epistemic game for young students
description: Bielaczyc and Ow introduce about-10-year-old Singapore students to collaborative knowledge building by framing online discussion as a multi-user knowledge-building ("epistemic") game in which players progressively improve tentative ideas proposed in response to a topic. In Knowledge Forum, postings are categorized by knowledge-building roles ("my theory," "I need to know," etc.), other students respond to or build on notes, and progress takes place through interaction among the notes, which serve as interactional resources for the group process.
requirements: Students must learn to enact effectively the categories and interactional moves of the game supported by the software
constraints: It takes years for teachers, students, schools, and school systems to adopt the necessary philosophy of knowledge building

refining tentative theories of scientific phenomena
examples: The scientific topic "How do we know if something is a living thing?" guides a particular group inquiry toward approaching established theories of the scientific community

article_title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
citation: Chan, C. K. K. (2011). Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9121-0
title: Knowledge-Building Teacher Network (KBTN) in Hong Kong
description: A teacher network funded by the Hong Kong Education Bureau since 2006, consisting of more than 50 teachers across primary and secondary schools. It uses a secondment scheme (50% release time) and later a university-school partnership scheme with teacher associates. The network connects researchers and teachers to implement and scale up knowledge building across 18-29 schools per year, spanning curriculum areas from science to liberal studies.
requirements: Education Bureau funding for teacher secondment and release time
University research collaboration and technology infrastructure support
constraints: Teacher participation fluctuated; some strong teachers stopped participating unexpectedly
target_learning_goals: Knowledge-building pedagogy implementation
Teacher professional development for CSCL
examples: Year 1: 18 schools, 25-30 teachers, 7 seconded teachers; Year 4: 29 schools, 50-60 teachers, 6 seconded teachers and 9 teacher associates
key_sources: Chan, C. K. K. (2011). Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-011-9121-0

article_title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
citation: Eddy Y.C. Lee, Carol K.K. Chan, & Jan van Aalst. (2006). Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-6844-4
title: Knowledge-building portfolios as assessment that characterizes and scaffolds collective knowledge advances
description: Knowledge-building portfolios are student-produced records in which learners select exemplary clusters of computer notes and write reflections explaining how the notes evidence knowledge building, guided by principles. Unlike conventional portfolios of individual best work, the article "pioneered the notion of knowledge-building portfolios for which students are asked to identify collective knowledge advances." A portfolio note is a "rise-above" note hyperlinked to referenced notes, and "A portfolio is a group accomplishment with multiple contributions from students—it shows that knowledge is distributed and it emerges through collective inquiry." The portfolio is designed to both measure and foster inquiry, mediating individual and group understanding through principles and reflections.
requirements: Students work in a Knowledge Forum database whose notes they can hyperlink, reference, and organize into clusters
A set of knowledge-building principles is provided as criteria for note selection and explanation
constraints: Developed and examined in a design research program with graduate, Grade 12, and grade-nine Geography classes in Hong Kong using Knowledge Forum
target_learners: secondary school students (grade-nine Geography students in this study)
target_learning_goals: collaborative inquiry and knowledge building
domain conceptual understanding
self- and community-assessment of knowledge advances
examples: Students prepared a portfolio of four clusters of notes with explanations, posted in the Assessment View, codeable on a 6-point rating scheme with inter-rater reliability .88
key_sources: Eddy Y.C. Lee, Carol K.K. Chan, & Jan van Aalst. (2006). Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building. Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-006-8997-6

article_title: Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement
citation: Yang, Y., van Aalst, J., Chan, C.K.K., & Tian, W. (2016). Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-016-9239-1
title: Knowledge Connections Analyzer (KCA)
description: The Knowledge Connections Analyzer (KCA) is a Web-based assessment tool that "queries the Knowledge Forum database to collect information on four intuitive questions related to knowledge building." It "displays quantitative data in pie charts and bar graphs and qualitative information in text-based tables." The tool uses social-media analogies such as friends and followers to analyze community collaboration. The study used the first two questions, focusing on community collaboration and synthesis/rise-above, to support reflective assessment among low-achieving students.
requirements: Requires a Knowledge Forum database with student discourse data
Requires prompt sheets to help students interpret the quantitative data generated
constraints: Only two of the four questions were used in this study due to available instructional time
Many students were initially unable to interpret KCA data productively
target_learning_goals: reflective assessment
collaborative knowledge building
metacognitive monitoring
examples: Students selected notes with many links and checked the content of linked notes to evaluate the appropriateness of the links

article_title: The richness of CSCL environments
citation: Ulrike Cress. (2020). The richness of CSCL environments. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09335-1
title: Knowledge Appropriation Model connecting scaffolded learning and knowledge maturing
description: The Knowledge Appropriation Model, developed by Ley and colleagues and applied by Rodríguez-Triana et al. to the Go-Lab teacher community, "integrates three processes: Knowledge maturing transforms individual knowledge to a collective level." Scaffolding practices support individuals who need help applying shared materials in concrete working situations, and through knowledge appropriation individuals become aware of existing knowledge, interact with others, refine ideas, and adapt existing solutions to new situations. The editorial describes it as a rich theoretical model describing circles of maturation and appropriation that includes processes at the individual level, the social level, and the interaction between the two.
requirements: The model was operationalized with process indicators (created, shared, co-edited, published, used ILSs; help requests; participation in activity events; reuse and refining) applied to shared platform resources.
constraints: The editorial notes the model was tested with quite simple statistics, placing the complexity in the conceptual model rather than the analysis.
target_learners: teachers in an online instructional design community
target_learning_goals: professional learning about instructional design for inquiry learning
examples: The study defined indicators for each process, such as "Indicators for knowledge maturing are the numbers of created, shared, co-edited, published and used ILSs", and traced implementation of about 40,000 ILSs.
key_sources: Ulrike Cress. (2020). The richness of CSCL environments. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09335-1

article_title: Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning
citation: María Jesús Rodríguez-Triana, Luis P. Prieto, Tobias Ley, Ton de Jong, Denis Gillet. (2020). Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning. International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-020-09331-5
title: Knowledge Appropriation Model (KAM)
description: The Knowledge Appropriation Model describes social practices of learning and knowledge creation in professional settings, based on sociocultural models of knowledge maturation and scaffolding. In this article KAM is the analytical framework used to map 12 practices — such as "Knowledge maturation practices lead to the transformation and maturation of knowledge" through sharing, co-creation, formalization and standardization; scaffolding practices of help-seeking, guidance and fading; and appropriation practices of awareness, adaptation and validation — onto traceable indicators in the Go-Lab community. The model assumes appropriation practices underlie both maturation and scaffolding, connecting collective knowledge with individual application.
requirements: Social practices must be observable through traces or interactions through which knowledge is collectively developed and individually applied
constraints: In this study only practices mediated by the Graasp platform could be traced; appropriation was operationalized only as reuse and edition of others' ILSs
target_learning_goals: adoption of inquiry-based learning pedagogy
teacher professional learning and knowledge creation
examples: The study mapped KAM practices onto Graasp log indicators across 40,235 ILSs and found maturation, scaffolding and appropriation traces associated with classroom adoption

article_title: Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis
citation: Xinran Zhu · Bodong Chen · David DeLiema. (2026). Advancing collaborative discourse through knowledge synthesis. Intern. J. Comput.-Support. Collab. Learn. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11412-025-09463-6
title: Knowledge synthesis in CSCL: connecting, analyzing, and integrating ideas from discourse to foster conceptual innovation
description: The article articulates knowledge synthesis (KS) as "the process of connecting, analyzing, and integrating ideas from collaborative discourse to foster conceptual innovation, generate novel knowledge, and create solutions". Unlike summarizing, synthesis-making moves beyond current explanations to create new concepts. The theory positions student-created synthesis artifacts as mediational tools that make emerging group knowledge visible and deepen ongoing discourse, situating KS relative to knowledge integration, web-mediated synthesis strategies, and Knowledge Building's "rise above".
requirements: Synthesis artifacts must be created from ideas represented in prior digital artifacts and then leveraged in new collaborative activity
Guidance outlining key components of effective synthesis, such as identifying common themes and exploring interconnections
constraints: The article notes insights about synthesis remain fragmented and underused in CSCL, with limited understanding of what makes a synthesis artifact effective
target_learners: graduate students in a teaching and learning course
target_learning_goals: advancing collaborative discourse
conceptual innovation and shared knowledge advancement
examples: In the study, students synthesized social annotation activity into individual artifacts and used them in group synthesis and application phases

article_title: Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty
citation: Olga Vogel, Marcel Hunecke. (2024). Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09653-5
title: Knowledge integration as a super-ordinate competency of inter- and transdisciplinary work built on four individual competencies
description: The article defines knowledge integration as "the cognitive ability to combine different disciplinary insights into a common knowledge base to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of a complex ITD problem". It treats knowledge integration as a super-ordinate competency building on specific competencies, drawing on Repko and Szostak's four-step process (identifying conflicts, creating common ground, constructing and testing a more comprehensive understanding). The study empirically links four individual competencies to this construct.
requirements: Individuals must engage with multiple disciplinary perspectives whose divergent insights create the unrelated knowledge structures to be merged
constraints: The construct is measured here by self-report; the article states the postulated competencies could not be assumed to causally impact knowledge integration
target_learners: economic-sector professionals working in inter- and transdisciplinary contexts
target_learning_goals: integrating knowledge from multiple disciplines and fields of practice into a common knowledge base
examples: The study operationalized the construct with the German version of Claus and Wiese's three-item knowledge integration scale, α = .830
key_sources: Olga Vogel, Marcel Hunecke. (2024). Fostering knowledge integration through individual competencies: the impacts of perspective taking, reflexivity, analogical reasoning and tolerance of ambiguity and uncertainty. Instructional Science. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-023-09653-5

article_title: The limits of curiosity? New evidence for the roles of metacognitive abilities and curiosity in learning
citation: Xiaoyun Chen, Katherine E. Twomey, Miranda Hayes, Gert Westermann. (2024). The limits of curiosity? New evidence for the roles of metacognitive abilities and curiosity in learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09407-9
title: Two distinct metacognitive confidence types: Knowledge Confidence and Correctness Confidence
description: The article identifies and separates two metacognitive appraisals that relate to curiosity in distinct ways. Knowledge Confidence is the subjective estimate of one's general prior knowledge state, while Correctness Confidence is the appraisal of the likelihood that a specific guess closes the knowledge gap. As the article states, "Knowledge Confidence is different from Correctness Confidence. The former emphasises the evaluation of one's general knowledge state", whereas the latter reflects "appraisal of a specific prediction". The study uses this distinction to show the two confidence types mediate curiosity differently and play different roles in learning.
requirements: Learners must make both a general prior-knowledge judgement and a confidence rating on a specific guess for the two appraisals to be measured separately
constraints: Distinction established with blurred object images in an online young-adult sample; the authors call for extension to other age groups and paradigms
target_learners: educators seeking to leverage metacognitive appraisal
target_learning_goals: metacognitive appraisal of knowledge states
curiosity-driven information seeking
recall of object names
examples: Participants answered "Do you know what this is?" (Yes/No/Not Sure), gave a best guess, rated guess confidence from 1 to 6, and rated curiosity for each of 60 blurred images
key_sources: Xiaoyun Chen, Katherine E. Twomey, Miranda Hayes, Gert Westermann. (2024). The limits of curiosity? New evidence for the roles of metacognitive abilities and curiosity in learning. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-024-09407-9

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Typology of knowledge: content, form, declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge
description: The authors define knowledge as used in cognitive psychology, encompassing the what, how, and when of learning. Knowledge of content includes factual and personal-experience knowledge one can name; knowledge of form enables distinguishing one thing from another by features. Each type includes declarative knowledge (what) and procedural knowledge (how), and the typology adds conditional knowledge, "the knowledge of when to apply knowledge of content or form," such as knowing not to exaggerate when reporting research results.
requirements: Distinguishing these knowledge types is needed to analyze what particular writing and reading tasks demand
constraints: The typology is applied to extended written discourse and imaginative literature, not to grammatical knowledge
target_learners: students learning to compose and interpret texts
target_learning_goals: knowing what, how, and when to apply knowledge in writing and reading tasks
key_sources: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543062003279

article_title: The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity
citation: Smagorinsky, P., & Smith, M. W. (1992). The Nature of Knowledge in Composition and Literary Understanding: The Question of Specificity. Review of Educational Research, 62(3), 279-305. http://rer.aera.net
title: Typology of knowledge: content, form, declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge
description: The authors define knowledge as used in cognitive psychology to encompass the what, how, and when of learning. Knowledge of content is "not merely one's factual knowledge of information" but also knowledge of personal experiences; knowledge of form "enables one to distinguish one thing from another according to their features." Each type can be declarative (what) or procedural (how), and conditional knowledge is "the knowledge of when to apply knowledge of content or form."
requirements: Distinguishing these knowledge types is needed to analyze what particular writing and reading tasks demand of learners.
target_learners: students in composition and literature instruction
target_learning_goals: knowing what, how, and when to apply knowledge in composing and reading
examples: The authors illustrate conditional knowledge: one might know how to exaggerate for humorous effect, but conditional knowledge should inform one not to exaggerate when reporting research results.

article_title: Fostering teenagers' assessment of information reliability: Effects of a classroom intervention focused on critical source dimensions
citation: Ana Pérez, Anna Potocki, Marc Stadtler, Mônica Macedo-Rouet, Johanna Paul, Ladislao Salmerón, Jean-François Rouet. (2018). Fostering Teenagers' Assessment of Information Reliability: Effects of a Classroom Intervention focused on Critical Source Dimensions. Learning and Instruction. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.learninstruc.2018.04.006
title: Knowledge application task: rating search-result links contrasted on three source dimensions
description: An assessment instrument in which students imagine searching for a topic and "rate on a Likert scale from 0 (certainly not) to 4 (certainly), whether they would consult or not several links". Author position, author motivation and media quality were manipulated to create four link types: good (reliable on all three dimensions), fair (two dimensions), poor (one), and bad (none), plus a filler link. The dependent variable was the mean normalized rating score from 0 to 1, with three counterbalanced topic versions.
requirements: Topic versions counterbalanced across phases and schools to prevent biases due to topic knowledge or interest
constraints: The distinction between more reliable (good, fair) and less reliable (poor, bad) links is described by the authors as merely indicative
target_learning_goals: applying source-dimension knowledge to judge whether to consult documents
examples: Topics included "The period of world history called Cold War", "Opinion polls in democratic societies", and "The health risks of electromagnetic waves emitted by mobile phones"

article_title: Lighting the wick in the candle of learning: generating a prediction stimulates curiosity
citation: Garvin Brod and Jasmin Breitwieser. (2019). Lighting the wick in the candle of learning: generating a prediction stimulates curiosity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0056-y
title: Knowledge-gap relevance account: prediction generation stimulates curiosity by increasing the relevance of the knowledge gap
description: The article advances an interpretation, building on Berlyne's arousal conjecture and Loewenstein's information-gap proposal, that "generating a prediction increases the relevance of the knowledge gap, i.e., the subjective value of the soon-to-be-learned information." The increased relevance plays out as enhanced arousal in anticipation and enhanced attention to the gap. The authors speculate that a key driver is a priori committing to a specific outcome, which goes beyond merely generating a response.
requirements: Generating a prediction before receiving feedback, so learners commit to a specific outcome before seeing the correct one
constraints: The article offers this as an interpretation and speculation, not a tested mechanism; the study cannot provide causal evidence for the effects of feedback on curiosity because the curiosity rating always took place before feedback
target_learning_goals: stimulating curiosity for factual knowledge to support memory encoding
examples: The experiment compared prediction generation with matched example generation, both followed by curiosity ratings, answer anticipation, and feedback
key_sources: Garvin Brod and Jasmin Breitwieser. (2019). Lighting the wick in the candle of learning: generating a prediction stimulates curiosity. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-019-0056-y

article_title: Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning
citation: Pammer-Schindler, V. & Rosé, C. (2021). Data-Related Ethics Issues in Technologies for Informal Professional Learning. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00259-x
title: KnowSelf activity logging and reflection prototype
description: KnowSelf is a Windows activity-log application that "collects time-stamped PC activity data, linked to web or file resources, identifies idle times, and visualizes the fragmentation of worktime". It supports manual time labeling into user-meaningful categories, note-taking, visualizations supporting reflection-on-action, and proactive prompts triggered at predetermined times or by user behavior such as long idleness. It was positively evaluated in two field studies with senior IT and strategy consultants.
requirements: Manual time labeling to sort automatically logged data into categories meaningful to the user
constraints: Centralized multi-device logging with centralized storage was strongly rejected by target users due to data sensitivity
target_learners: knowledge workers and consultants in workplace settings
target_learning_goals: time management reflection and improvement
examples: Two field studies in a German medium-sized company with reasonably senior IT and strategy consultants positively evaluated KnowSelf and regular review of time use

article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes
citation: Andrew M. Olney, Stephen B. Gilbert, Kelly Rivers. (2021). Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00277-9

Albó, Barria-Pineda, Brusilovsky, and Hernández-Leo "describe a knowledge-based learning analytics dashboard and how course designers used it to select learning activities that balance coverage and practice opportunities for knowledge components" in their paper "Knowledge-based Design Analytics for Authoring Courses with Smart Learning Content." The editorial classifies it as "an adaptive authoring system" that orchestrates both adaptive and non-adaptive learning activities.

constraints: Classified as adaptive authoring of non-adaptive content in Table 1

examples: Course designers used the dashboard to select learning activities balancing coverage and practice opportunities for knowledge components

article_title: Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy
citation: Lechuga, C. G., & Doroudi, S. (2023). Three Algorithms for Grouping Students: A Bridge Between Personalized Tutoring System Data and Classroom Pedagogy. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-022-00309-y
title: Knowledge Space Theory and the outer fringe as a multidimensional readiness construct underlying ALEKS grouping
description: ALEKS's domain model is based on Knowledge Space Theory, a combinatoric and probabilistic model of knowledge assessment in which a student's knowledge state is the set of items the student can complete correctly unaided, and a knowledge structure captures prerequisite relationships among items. The outer fringe is defined conceptually as "the set of items the student is ready to learn," tracked over hundreds of discrete items; the article notes the inner and outer fringes are "somewhat related to Vygotsky's (1930–1934/1978) notion of Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD)." The outer fringe serves as a pillar for all three grouping methods.
requirements: An adaptive assessment that identifies each student's state, unknown items, and outer fringe from a course structure of typically 300 to 600 items
constraints: Unlike Vygotsky's ZPD, ALEKS assumes two students with the same exact knowledge state always have the same outer fringe and does not predict differences in learning pace
target_learners: K-12, higher education, and independent learners using ALEKS courses in mathematics, chemistry, statistics, and accounting
target_learning_goals: Determining student knowledge and readiness to learn individual course items for individualized learning paths and grouping
examples: The article uses outer fringes with respect to a module as the basis of the overlap metrics evaluating the within-module grouping method.

article_title: Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy
citation: Ormel, B. J. B., Pareja Roblin, N. N., McKenney, S. E., Voogt, J. M., & Pieters, J. M. (2012). Research–practice interactions as reported in recent design studies: still promising, still hazy. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-012-9261-6
title: Knowledge produced by design research may be declarative, procedural, or observable
description: Building on previous work (Edelson 2002; Van den Akker 1999), the article indicates that "the nature of knowledge produced by design research may be one or more of the following: declarative (describing products, concepts or theories); procedural (informing how to take action); or observable (empirical findings or experiences)". Each of these has the potential to contribute to theory building, and knowledge produced may also be characterized by its focus, for example on teaching, learning and/or resources. This typology is used to code the public knowledge produced in each of the 18 reviewed projects.
requirements: Knowledge produced must be classifiable as declarative, procedural, or observable for coding
constraints: This study aims to identify and describe immediate interactions between research and practice and does not explicitly aim to portray broader dissemination and use of the research findings
target_learning_goals: characterizing knowledge outputs of design research
examples: Observable knowledge was found in all 18 studies, including students' comments, learning gains, and teachers' opinions.

article_title: Self-Directed Learning in Health Professions Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
citation: Wilkes S., Maggio L. A., Martin P. C., Melton J., Zheng B. (2026). Self-Directed Learning in Health Professions Education: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Perspectives on Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.5334/pme.2128
title: Knowles' andragogy as the foundational framework for self-directed learning in health professions education
description: The review frames self-directed learning primarily through Knowles' andragogy, defining SDL as "a process in which individuals take the initiative, with or without the help of others, in diagnosing their learning needs, formulating learning goals, identifying resources for learning, choosing and implementing appropriate learning strategies, and evaluating learning outcomes." The framework delineates three essential components: educators as facilitators rather than content sources, learner involvement in determining needs and resources, and learner direction of implementation and evaluation. The review uses these components as coding criteria and acknowledges that empirical evidence for andragogy itself is limited.
requirements: SDL interventions must involve learners in diagnosing learning needs, formulating goals, identifying resources, and evaluating outcomes to fully embody the framework
constraints: The authors note empirical evidence for andragogy itself is limited and its assumptions (e.g., that all adult learners inherently seek autonomy) have been critiqued
target_learners: health professions learners (medical, nursing, dental, allied health students and trainees)
target_learning_goals: learner autonomy, self-assessment, lifelong learning

article_title: Analysis of Nurses' and Physicians' Attitudes, Knowledge, and Perceptions toward Fever in Children: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis.
citation: Vicens-Blanes, F., Miró-Bonet, R., & Molina-Mula, J. (2021). Analysis of Nurses' and Physicians' Attitudes, Knowledge, and Perceptions toward Fever in Children: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph182312444
title: Three-variable taxonomy (knowledge, attitudes, perceptions) for classifying outcomes of nurses' fever-management education
description: The review organizes the evaluation of educational programs for nurses around three outcome classes. Knowledge covers "understanding of fever physiology, fever management, and antipyretic drugs or measures"; attitudes cover changes in clinical practice with a febrile child, performance against febrile convulsions, and health education provided to parents; perceptions cover how parents, nursing colleagues, and physicians influence care of a febrile child and how much control professionals have over management. The meta-analysis pools studies separately within these three classes.
requirements: Studies must evaluate an educational program for nurses related to fever care for children and measure at least one of the three outcome classes.
For the quantitative synthesis, articles must report at least two statistical measures of the variables, shared through mean and standard deviation.
constraints: The review states the variables are "difficult to quantify", and some included programs used unvalidated questionnaires, which may restrict validity.
target_learners: nurses in hospital and community pediatric settings
target_learning_goals: knowledge of fever physiology and management
attitudes toward fever management practice
perceptions of control over febrile child management
examples: The review classified 41 articles by the variable they measured and pooled five program evaluations separately for knowledge, attitudes, and perceptions.

article_title: Research Learning Communities: Evaluation Report and Executive Summary
citation: Dr Jo Rose, Professor Sally Thomas, Dr Lei Zhang, Dr Anna Edwards, Dr Andres Augero, Ms Pooneh Roney. (2017). Research Learning Communities: Evaluation report and executive summary. Education Endowment Foundation. https://www.educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk
title: Knowledge mobilisation as a framework for embedding research use in schools
description: The report frames RLC within the concept of knowledge mobilisation, defined as "the process through which evidence is produced through research, then made accessible to, and implemented by, practitioners". The framework holds that simply summarising research is not effective; evidence must be transformed for practitioner use, requiring collaboration between researchers and teachers beyond knowledge exchange. RLC applies this by facilitating teachers to develop their own research-informed cultures appropriate to their school contexts, acknowledging contextual complexity rather than working in spite of it.
requirements: practitioners need to develop skills in engaging with, and conducting, their own research
an infrastructure for knowledge mobilisation to support teachers in using evidence
constraints: there is no guarantee that engaging with research-based initiatives will result in improvements in educational outcomes
target_learning_goals: teachers' critical engagement with research evidence
research-informed teaching practice
examples: RLC workshops built capacity in research methods and supported schools to collect baseline data, trial approaches and measure impact

article_title: Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms
citation: Balım, A. G., İnel-Ekici, D., & Özcan, E. (2016). Concept Cartoons Supported Problem Based Learning Method in Middle School Science Classrooms. Journal of Education and Learning, 5(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/jel.v5n2p272
title: Knowledge-daily life relating open ended questions instrument
description: A five-question open-ended instrument prepared to assess students' knowledge of matter and heat in daily life, validated by three academics and one science teacher (expert agreement .86 for scientific knowledge adequacy and .90 for language rules). Scoring used a four-point system from 0 to 3 points per question, and inter-expert agreement was checked with nine experts, yielding an "aggrement correlation coefficient" of .82 and a Pearson correlation of .94.
requirements: expert validation and pilot testing with 35 students before final use
target_learning_goals: relating science knowledge (matter and heat) with daily life situations
examples: Sample items ask why a jar lid expands in hot water, why wooden seats feel less cold than stone or metal, and why thermos linings are shiny

article_title: The Effect of Carrying out Writing to Learn Activities on Academic Success of Fifth Grade Students in Secondary School on the Subject of "Force and Motion"

Universal Journal of Educational Research 5(5): 744-749. https://doi.org/10.13189/ujer.2017.050506
title: Knowledge-telling versus knowledge-transforming models of writing-to-learn
description: The article presents Bereiter and Scardamalia's two models of writing-to-learn. In the "knowledge-telling model", writing is "linear and away from socio -cultural interaction" and achievement depends on stored memory. The "knowledge-transforming model" instead "encourages educators in cases such as setting goals, identifying readers, thinking, negotiating, strategic planning, review and reflection" and "is mediated by an active problem solving". The article uses this contrast to frame why non-traditional writing activities may facilitate critical thinking and conceptual change.
requirements: Writing used to promote learning, student-teacher interaction during writing, writing playing a major role in course grades, substantial text production, and limited class enrollment, as listed by Yore, Hand & Prain
target_learning_goals: science conceptual understanding
scientific literacy
critical thinking
examples: The study's poem-writing and journal-keeping activities are offered as instances of writing-to-learn activities that facilitate critical thinking and conceptual change rather than traditional writing

article_title: How Do Openers Contribute to Student Learning?
citation: Zertuche, A., Gerard, L., & Linn, M. C. (2012). How do Openers Contribute to Student Learning? International Electronic Journal of Elementary Education, 5(1), 79-92. http://www.iejee.com
title: Knowledge integration perspective on learning
description: The knowledge integration perspective holds that "learners hold multiple conflicting ideas about scientific phenomenon" and that learners "can deliberately sort out, link, and critique their ideas when making sense of new scientific phenomena". It guides the design of the Openers, curriculum, and assessments in this study, in contrast to the absorption-model question-response-evaluation approach typical of classroom Openers. Openers built on it elicit ideas, add ideas, distinguish ideas, and integrate ideas.
requirements: Providing opportunities for students to compare alternative ideas to their own, develop criteria for sorting out ideas, and reflect on their ideas
target_learning_goals: Understanding chemical reactions, including conservation of mass, bond breaking, and reaction progression
examples: The researcher-designed Opener elicited predictions, had students vote, discuss in groups of 4 while revisiting the hydrogen combustion visualization, re-vote, and justify choices before revising their drawings.

title: K-N-W-S graphic organizer intervention package with video modeling via TeachLivE avatar
description: The intervention package consisted of the K-N-W-S graphic organizer, three pre-recorded standardized validated videos, and a packet of daily word problems. The researcher pre-recorded teaching each step of the K-N-W-S strategy to a TeachLivE avatar, providing a "scripted model and strict fidelity". Three special education experts validated each video for content and clarity. Students practiced two word problems per day over nine consecutive school days.
requirements: A teacher reads a script to introduce videos and word problems each day while students practice applying the graphic organizer
constraints: The videos were validated for content but not for level of student engagement or production value
target_learners: fourth and fifth grade students with disabilities in inclusive classrooms
target_learning_goals: mathematical word problem solving using multiplication and division problems
examples: The daily word problems were aligned with the pre/posttest and adapted from the Go Math! curriculum, covering grouping or partitioning, rate, price, and multiplicative comparison problems

title: K-N-W-S graphic organizer strategy for mathematical word problems
description: The K-N-W-S strategy is a mathematics graphic organizer comprised of four steps: identifying what students "KNOW (K) from the information stated in the problem", what information is "NOT (N) need[ed]", "WHAT (W) exactly does this problem ask me to find", and what "STRATEGY (S) or operation will I use to solve this problem". It is intended to support students in planning, organizing, and analyzing word problems in a structured, visual, and concrete way.
requirements: The organizer should be paired with strong, direct instruction of mathematical concepts
constraints: The K-N-W-S graphic organizer had not yet been explored with students with ASD prior to this study
target_learners: students with disabilities solving mathematical word problems
target_learning_goals: planning, organizing, and analyzing mathematical word problems
examples: Students were provided with a copy of the graphic organizer along with daily word problems and instructed to use it

title: Knowledge management tool categories supporting blended learning
description: The article lists categories of knowledge management tools that support blended learning, stating "Following categories of knowledge management tools support blended learning": content portal technologies, collaborative filtering techniques, search engines and text retrieval, directory technologies and expertise locators, virtual synchronous classrooms, digital content asset management systems, web-based content management systems, electronic document management systems, digital library technology, and knowledge map software. collaboration
knowledge sharing

description: The article frames the need for EBD education within the concept of 'knowledge translation,' which "seeks to transform research findings into practical applications that enhance healthcare outcomes." constraints: Barriers include vast volume of research, variability in evidence quality, conflicting findings, scientific illiteracy and imbalance between knowledge production and effective dissemination

article_title: Readiness for self-directed learning among undergraduate medical students in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during COVID-19, Pakistan.
citation: Hassan KE, Sethi A, Junaid SM, Khattak T, Khattak M. (2025). Readiness for self-directed learning among undergraduate medical students in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa during COVID-19, Pakistan. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-06745-3
title: Knowles' definition of self-directed learning and Garrison's SDL model
description: The article frames self-directed learning using Knowles' definition of SDL as "a process in which individuals take the initiative, with or without the help of others, in diagnosing their learning needs, formulating learning goals, identifying human and material resources for learning, choosing and implementing appropriate learning strategies, and evaluating learning outcomes". It also cites Garrison's model of self-directed learning, which "prioritizes motivation, self-management, and self-monitoring". The article uses these accounts to argue that incorporating SDL competence into medical education curricula is crucial for achieving learning goals.
requirements: Students take responsibility for and control of their own learning, with teachers fostering SDL by encouraging students, promoting reflection, and utilizing strategies like situated learning and problem-solving
constraints: The article notes challenges like assessing progress and managing time in implementing SDL
target_learning_goals: lifelong learning
self-directed diagnosis of learning needs and evaluation of learning outcomes
examples: The study operationalized SDL readiness levels (good, average, poor) on the SRSSDL against these definitions

article_title: Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage?
citation: Burgess A, Kalman E, Haq I, Leaver A, Roberts C, Bleasel J. (2020). Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02024-5
title: Knowledge reconsolidation framework for understanding learning in TBL
description: The article applies the 'knowledge reconsolidation' conceptual framework proposed by Schmidt et al. (2019) to understand interprofessional learning within TBL. It states that "there are four psychological mechanisms that enable knowledge reconsolidation during the TBL process": retrieval practice during the IRAT, peer elaboration during the TRAT, feedback following the TRAT, and transfer of learning during problem-solving activities. The authors use these four themes to organise their discussion of students' interprofessional learning.
requirements: TBL sessions structured with IRAT, TRAT, facilitator feedback, and clinical problem-solving activities so each mechanism can occur
constraints: The framework is applied as a lens for discussing findings in a single pilot session; the article does not test the framework itself
target_learners: health professional students (Year 1 medical and Year 2 physiotherapy students)
target_learning_goals: interprofessional collaboration
clinical reasoning
consolidation of prior knowledge
examples: The article maps retrieval practice to the IRAT, peer elaboration to the TRAT, feedback to facilitator clarification after the TRAT, and transfer of learning to the clinical problem-solving activities
key_sources: Burgess A, Kalman E, Haq I, Leaver A, Roberts C, Bleasel J. (2020). Interprofessional team-based learning (TBL): how do students engage? BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02024-5
